In the tower block, the WhatsApp group "Floor 9 Aunties" has forty-two members. Mrs Okafor, who has lived there longest, posts each morning: who needs a lift to the clinic, whose son has a job interview. When the lift broke for a week, members took turns carrying shopping for Mr Lindqvist, the retired sailor on the top floor. "We don't keep accounts," says Mrs Okafor, "but everyone knows who helps." New tenants are added only after someone has "met them properly". Last year a young man was removed from the group after he refused to lend his ladder.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a council housing block in a European city.

Describe, with examples from the text, how the residents support one another. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: They use a WhatsApp group; Mrs Okafor posts daily needs (lifts to the clinic, job interviews); members took turns carrying Mr Lindqvist's shopping when the lift broke; no accounts are kept; new tenants are admitted after being "met properly".

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I spent eighteen months on night shifts at the delivery depot, sorting parcels and later riding with drivers. My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. If I join the union, my cousin's company won't give me shifts." I recorded 46 interviews and kept a diary of the shifts I worked. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): from the introduction to an ethnography of delivery drivers in Berlin.

With reference to the concept of power, analyse how the anthropologist's methods support the argument in the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Long-term participant observation in the same shifts shows the work from within and builds rapport (Kemal's frank answer); interviews give drivers' own explanations; Kemal's statement directly illustrates the ambivalence (control/freedom) and reveals kinship ties (cousin's company) that shape decisions – evidence for the argument that platform power is experienced ambivalently.

Observation notes, Saturday 10.00–11.30, public library reading room. 10.04: A man in a suit chooses the table nearest the window and spreads three newspapers across it. 10.20: Two teenagers sit at the end of the same table; he moves one newspaper closer to himself without looking up. 10.41: A librarian walks past and says "Good morning, Mr Haddad." 10.55: An older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices; they put on earphones. 11.12: The man leaves; the teenagers spread out their books across the whole table within two minutes.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): observation notes written by a student in a public library.

With reference to space, place and time, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Ong's Flexible Citizenship. Keep the comparison running throughout rather than treating each case separately.
items.answer: Text: Space is claimed through objects (newspapers, books) and bodily signals rather than words; familiarity and recognition (the librarian knows Mr Haddad) give him authority over the "best" table; the teenagers negotiate by adjusting behaviour (earphones) and claim space once he leaves. Space becomes place through regular use, status and informal rules. Ethnography – Aihwa Ong, Flexible Citizenship: The Cultural Logics of Transnationality (1999), among wealthy Chinese business families moving between Hong Kong, South-East Asia and North America (1990s): "Astronaut" fathers commute across the Pacific while "parachute kids" study abroad, stretching family life across space. Comparison: similarities and differences in how space, place and time is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

The welfare office in Rotterdam introduced a "risk score" last year. Caseworker Annelies shows me the dashboard: applicants are coloured green, amber or red. "I don't know how it decides," she admits. "But if it's red, I must ask for six extra documents." She points out that many red cases live in two postcodes. Mr Yilmaz, an applicant in red, arrives with a folder of documents in plastic sleeves. "My neighbour told me to bring everything," he says. "The computer does not know us, so we must show it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a municipal welfare office in the Netherlands.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Welfare data and applicants' status are confidential; the anthropologist needs permission from the municipality, consent from applicants and staff, and must avoid making identifiable claims about postcodes that could stigmatise neighbourhoods. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that symbolic healing is as effective as biomedical treatment. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Their efficacy cannot be compared on one scale; symbolic healing addresses meaning and suffering, biomedicine biological disease.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: symbolic healing relieves suffering and anxiety (Lévi-Strauss); placebo research shows meaning has physiological effects; biomedicine is clearly more effective for infections and surgery; efficacy is defined differently in each system. items.answer: Communities adapted care and burial practices, developing safer burials and local quarantine, which Richards calls "people's science".

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as De León's The Land of Open Graves and Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, compare and contrast the role of materiality in the use and exchange of objects.
items.answer: De León's The Land of Open Graves (on the US–Mexico border in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, through the Undocumented Migration Project): De León combines archaeology, forensic science and ethnography, analysing discarded water bottles, backpacks and clothing as traces of migrants' experience. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): Kula valuables are rarely worn or used; their value lies in their histories and the names of past holders, so objects carry social biographies and prestige rather than utility. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far materiality is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Fadiman's The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down and Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, compare and contrast the role of power in the body and culturally specific illness.
items.answer: Fadiman's The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down (about Lia Lee, a Hmong child with epilepsy, her family and her doctors in Merced, California (1980s)): Doctors' complex drug regimes and the removal of Lia into foster care for non-compliance show biomedicine overriding a family's explanatory model. Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)): She describes the "everyday violence" of poverty, in which hunger is medicalised as nervos and treated with tranquillisers and vitamins, hiding the political causes of suffering. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

Every December the elders of the Nakamura neighbourhood association repair the paper lanterns for the shrine festival. This year the young men who carry the portable shrine asked to add LED strips. Mr Kato, who has led the festival for thirty years, refused: "The flame must flicker. That is how the kami know we are here." His granddaughter, filming on her phone, rolled her eyes. "He says the same thing about the music, but he changed the route when the new road came." In the end, the LEDs were allowed on the trucks that follow the shrine, but not on the shrine itself.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood shrine festival in urban Japan.

Describe, with examples from the text, the disagreement about the festival lanterns. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The doctor at the district clinic tells Grandfather Osei that his blood pressure is "very high" and gives him tablets. On the walk home he tells his grandson that the pressure comes from "thinking too much" since his land was taken by his nephew. He takes the tablets only on days when he has quarrelled. His grandson, a nursing student, explains that the tablets must be taken daily. "The tablets are for the body," the old man replies. "The thinking needs a family meeting." The following week, the elders call the nephew to a meeting.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural district in Ghana.

Explain, with close reference to the text, how the text illustrates differing explanatory models of sickness. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: The doctor's model locates hypertension in the body and prescribes daily medication (disease); Grandfather Osei's model links his illness to a social conflict over land (personalistic and social cause) and so adapts the treatment; he combines biomedicine with a family meeting to treat the social cause, illustrating Kleinman's disease/illness distinction and medical pluralism within the popular sector.

I spread the family tree on the floor of the courtyard. Grandmother Sita corrected me at once: her late husband's brother's son should not be on the same line as her own sons "because they eat separately since the quarrel". She asked me to remove a woman I had included as a cousin: "She married outside; we do not count her." Her granddaughter, Priya, quietly added the woman back when Sita went inside. Later I photographed the family; Sita insisted that the sons stand at the front and the daughters-in-law behind.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a joint household in rural Nepal.

Compare the significance of classification in the text with its significance in Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Keep the comparison running throughout rather than treating each case separately.
items.answer: Text: Both methods are not neutral records: the genealogy is shaped by present relationships (commensality, quarrels) and by judgements about who "counts" (exclusion after marriage outside), and different members (Sita, Priya) contest it; the photograph stages hierarchy by gender and generation. The methods reveal classification and power within the household. Ethnography – Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013), with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005): Farm labour is organised in an ethnic-citizenship hierarchy: white and Asian American owners, then mestizo Mexican supervisors, with undocumented Triqui pickers at the bottom doing the most physically damaging work. Comparison: similarities and differences in how classification is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

The cleaners at the hotel start before dawn. They are paid per room, not per hour, so Fatou never takes the lunch break written in her contract. She keeps her own list of "good floors" where guests leave tips and "bad floors" of business travellers. The supervisor, Mme Laurent, gives the good floors to the women who bring her pastries on Fridays. When the hotel advertised its "green policy" of not washing towels daily, Fatou laughed: "Green for them, more rooms for us."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a hotel in Paris.

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that classification is primarily a tool of the powerful. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Powerful institutions shape classification most strongly, but categories are also resources for those seeking change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: states and experts create categories to govern (Scott, Dirks); risk-group labels stigmatise the poor (Farmer); marginalised groups use categories for solidarity and rights (Dalit, hijra); everyday classifications are made by everyone. Suitable ethnographies include Dirks's Castes of Mind, Srinivas's work on Sanskritisation and the dominant caste, Farmer's AIDS and Accusation. items.stem: Using Petryna's Life Exposed and Richards's Ebola, compare the ways in which power is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Petryna's Life Exposed (in Ukraine after the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster): Scientific and bureaucratic commissions determined whose illnesses counted as Chernobyl-related, controlling access to welfare. Richards's Ebola (in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2015 West African Ebola epidemic): Top-down responses that ignored local knowledge produced distrust, while co-operation with chiefs and communities proved more effective. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Lock's Encounters with Aging and Martin's The Woman in the Body, compare and contrast the role of power in the body and culturally specific illness.
items.answer: Lock's Encounters with Aging (comparing middle-aged women in Japan with women in Canada and the United States): North American medicine framed menopause as a deficiency disease requiring hormone therapy, whereas Japanese doctors placed more emphasis on women's family duties, so medical models carried moral and gendered expectations. Martin's The Woman in the Body (among women in Baltimore, USA, and in medical textbooks): Middle-class women tended to accept the medical model of their bodies, while working-class women more often resisted it. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

At the end of Ramadan, the Hassan family invites the neighbours to break the fast. Mrs Hassan has bought a separate set of plates "for guests who drink". Mr Oduya from next door brings a cake; she thanks him warmly and places it on the guest table. Later, her teenage daughter Yasmin whispers that the cake contains gelatine. Mrs Hassan smiles: "We do not need to eat it to accept it." At the end of the evening, she sends the leftover cake home with the Oduya children.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood in Manchester, England.

Describe the food practices at the Hassans' evening meal, as presented in the text. Organise your answer as a series of clearly separated descriptive points.
items.answer: The Hassans break the fast with neighbours; Mrs Hassan uses a separate set of plates for guests who drink alcohol; Mr Oduya brings a cake, which is placed on the guest table; Yasmin notices it contains gelatine; the family does not eat it but accepts it and sends leftovers back with the Oduya children.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the village, every household sends a son to the annual repair of the irrigation channel. Nobody is paid. The work lasts three days and ends with a feast at which the eldest man of each lineage receives the first portion of meat. Thabo, home from his job in Johannesburg, paid a cousin to go in his place this year. The elders accepted the money but placed Thabo's family last in the line for the feast. "The channel brings water to all," the headman told me. "When a family does not dig, the water still comes, but the respect does not."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural village in Lesotho.

Explain how a functionalist might explain the channel repair, and what the text suggests about the limits of that explanation, using one or more anthropological concepts. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: A functionalist would argue the collective work meets the material need for water (Malinowski) and maintains social structure and solidarity, with the feast reaffirming lineage seniority (Radcliffe-Brown). But Thabo's substitution shows change from migrant wage labour and money entering obligations, and the sanction on his family shows tension and negotiation that an equilibrium model underplays.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the tower block, the WhatsApp group "Floor 9 Aunties" has forty-two members. Mrs Okafor, who has lived there longest, posts each morning: who needs a lift to the clinic, whose son has a job interview. When the lift broke for a week, members took turns carrying shopping for Mr Lindqvist, the retired sailor on the top floor. "We don't keep accounts," says Mrs Okafor, "but everyone knows who helps." New tenants are added only after someone has "met them properly". Last year a young man was removed from the group after he refused to lend his ladder.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a council housing block in a European city.

Compare and contrast the role of social relations in the text with social relations in one ethnography you have studied, such as Geertz's "Deep Play". Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: The group is a network that redistributes help through generalised reciprocity ("we don't keep accounts") yet reputation tracks who helps; Mrs Okafor's long residence gives her status and a coordinating role; admission and removal (the ladder) show boundaries and sanctions that enforce obligations. Ethnography – Clifford Geertz, "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" (1972; reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958): Men bet on the cocks of their own kin group or village and never against them, so patterns of betting map kinship, alliance and rivalry. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Big question: "Is change a threat to cultural identity, or a condition of it?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of identity and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Bourgois's In Search of Respect.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies identity explicitly and uses ethnography: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

Observation notes, Saturday 10.00–11.30, public library reading room. 10.04: A man in a suit chooses the table nearest the window and spreads three newspapers across it. 10.20: Two teenagers sit at the end of the same table; he moves one newspaper closer to himself without looking up. 10.41: A librarian walks past and says "Good morning, Mr Haddad." 10.55: An older woman asks the teenagers to lower their voices; they put on earphones. 11.12: The man leaves; the teenagers spread out their books across the whole table within two minutes.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): observation notes written by a student in a public library.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: The student recorded a real name (Mr Haddad) heard in public, which should be removed; library users did not consent, so notes must avoid identifying details; permission from library staff is advisable; the student should reflect on their own presence. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "Local knowledge is as important as biomedical knowledge in controlling epidemics." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: communities adapted burial practices to stop Ebola (Richards); trust determines whether interventions are accepted; biomedical knowledge identified pathogens, vaccines and treatments; local knowledge can include harmful practices or rumours. Suitable ethnographies include Richards's Ebola, Farmer's AIDS and Accusation, Lindenbaum's Kuru Sorcery. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Both are essential: biomedical tools are effective only when combined with local knowledge and trust. items.stem: With reference to John Janzen, The Quest for Therapy in Lower Zaire (1978), explain how the key concept of social relations helps us to understand the choices people make when seeking treatment.
items.answer: Decisions about treatment were taken not by the patient alone but by a "therapy management group" of kin who negotiated which healers to consult.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Barth's Ethnic Groups and Boundaries and Bowker and Star's Sorting Things Out, compare and contrast the role of identity in struggles over social categories.
items.answer: Barth's Ethnic Groups and Boundaries (in a comparative theory of ethnicity): Barth argued that ethnic identity is maintained by boundaries – processes of inclusion and exclusion – rather than by "the cultural stuff" a group contains. Bowker and Star's Sorting Things Out (on classification systems such as the International Classification of Diseases and apartheid South Africa's race classification): People "torque" between categories: their lives are twisted when an official category does not fit their biography, as with families split by apartheid reclassification. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far identity is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Explain how Fadiman's The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down illustrates the concept of culture. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Lia's parents understood her seizures as qaug dab peg – "the spirit catches you and you fall down" – a loss of soul that might also mark a future shaman, while doctors diagnosed epilepsy.

items.stem: Compare and contrast De León's The Land of Open Graves and Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific as accounts of the use and exchange of objects, focusing on the key concept of materiality.
items.answer: De León's The Land of Open Graves (on the US–Mexico border in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, through the Undocumented Migration Project): De León combines archaeology, forensic science and ethnography, analysing discarded water bottles, backpacks and clothing as traces of migrants' experience. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): Kula valuables are rarely worn or used; their value lies in their histories and the names of past holders, so objects carry social biographies and prestige rather than utility. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far materiality is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
